lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: You know the old man — the really old one, I mean — Eucrates, the rich one? No children, but about fifty thousand people hunting his estate?
lines.note: Pluto opens with the conspiratorial air of a building manager about to bend a rule. 'About fifty thousand' is Lucian's comic hyperbole — keep it deadpan.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: The man from Sicyon? Yes. What about him?

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Leave him alive, Hermes. He's had ninety years — give him another ninety on top. More, if possible. But his little flatterers — Charinus the young one, Damon, the whole crowd — bring them down. One after another.
lines.note: The reversal is the joke: Pluto ordering more life for the old man and death for the young heirs. Deliver it like a memo.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: That would seem a bit irregular.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: On the contrary — it's the most just thing imaginable. What exactly have these men suffered, that they go around praying for his death and grabbing at money that isn't remotely theirs? And the truly repellent part is that while they're praying for exactly that, they're all sweetness and devotion to his face. When he's ill, everyone knows perfectly well what they're hoping for — and yet they go right ahead and promise sacrifices if he recovers. The whole performance is extraordinarily elaborate. So: let him be immortal. And let them go on ahead of him, having gawped at his fortune for nothing.
lines.note: Pluto builds slowly here — this is his one genuine speech of wit in the collection. The rhythm should feel like a judge summarising the charge before delivering the verdict.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: They'll get what they deserve — conniving lot. And he plays them brilliantly, keeps them hoping, always looks like he's about to drop and then turns out to be in better health than men half his age. Meanwhile they've already divided the inheritance among themselves in private — living the dream, as far as they're concerned.
lines.note: Hermes is more amused here than put-upon — he has watched this particular game many times.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Then let him shed his old age like Iolaus and be young again. And let them leave their fantasy fortune behind — right in the middle of all their lovely expectations — and come down here. Bad men. Badly dead.
lines.note: 'Bad men, badly dead' — κακοὶ κακῶς — is the formal curse formula repurposed as a dry administrative sentence. Short, flat delivery.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Leave it to me, Pluto — I'll bring them down for you one by one, in order. There are seven of them, I think.
lines.note: Hermes shifts into logistics mode. He has his list.

lines.speaker: Pluto
lines.text: Bring them. And the old man can see each one off personally — a new young man again, sending them on their way.
lines.note: Final line: the image of the rejuvenated Eucrates playing cheerful host as his heirs file past to the ferry. Pluto delivers it straight.
